# Model Usage

The `Model` class in Tortoise ORM is the core abstraction for defining database entities. It provides a high-level, Pythonic interface for working with database tables, including field definitions, relationships, query building, and asynchronous operations.

## Defining a Model

To define a model, create a class that inherits from `tortoise.models.Model` and define fields as class attributes. Each field corresponds to a database column.

```python
from tortoise import Model, fields

class User(Model):
    id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
    name = fields.CharField(max_length=50)
    email = fields.CharField(max_length=100, unique=True)
    created_at = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now_add=True)
```

### Meta Options

The `Meta` inner class allows you to configure model behavior at the database level.

```python
class User(Model):
    id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
    name = fields.CharField(max_length=50)

    class Meta:
        table = "users"
        app = "myapp"
        abstract = False
        ordering = ["-created_at"]
        unique_together = ("name", "email")
        indexes = ("name",)
        table_description = "User accounts with their details"
```

- `table`: The database table name (default: lowercase model name).
- `app`: The app name (used for migrations and routing).
- `abstract`: If `True`, the model is not created in the database and serves as a base for other models.
- `ordering`: Default ordering for queries (e.g., `["-created_at"]`).
- `unique_together`: Tuple of field names that must be unique together.
- `indexes`: List of field names to create database indexes on.
- `table_description`: Optional description of the table.

## Fields

Fields define the structure of your model and map to database columns. Common field types include:

- `IntField`: Integer values.
- `CharField`: Variable-length strings (max_length required).
- `TextField`: Large text fields.
- `BooleanField`: Boolean values.
- `DateTimeField`: Date and time values.
- `FloatField`: Floating-point numbers.
- `JSONField`: JSON data storage.

### Field Options

Most fields support common options:

- `null`: Allow `None` values (default: `False`).
- `default`: Default value (can be a callable).
- `unique`: Enforce uniqueness.
- `index`: Create a database index.
- `generated`: Whether the field is auto-generated (e.g., primary key).

```python
class Product(Model):
    id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
    name = fields.CharField(max_length=100, unique=True)
    price = fields.DecimalField(max_digits=10, decimal_places=2, default=0.0)
    description = fields.TextField(null=True)
    created_at = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    updated_at = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now=True)
```

## Relationships

Tortoise supports various types of relationships between models.

### Foreign Key (One-to-Many)

```python
class User(Model):
    id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
    name = fields.CharField(max_length=50)

class Post(Model):
    id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
    title = fields.CharField(max_length=100)
    user = fields.ForeignKeyField("models.User", related_name="posts")
```

- `ForeignKeyField`: Defines a foreign key to another model.
- `related_name`: Name used to access related objects from the related model.

### One-to-One

```python
class Profile(Model):
    id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
    user = fields.OneToOneField("models.User", on_delete=fields.CASCADE)
    bio = fields.TextField()
```

### Many-to-Many

```python
class Tag(Model):
    id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
    name = fields.CharField(max_length=50)

class Article(Model):
    id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
    title = fields.CharField(max_length=100)
    tags = fields.ManyToManyField("models.Tag", related_name="articles")
```

## Querying

Models support a rich query API via `QuerySet`.

### Creating Instances

```python
user = await User.create(name="Alice", email="alice@example.com")
```

### Filtering

```python
users = await User.filter(name="Alice")
users = await User.filter(name__contains="Ali")
users = await User.filter(id__in=[1, 2, 3])
```

### Chaining Queries

```python
users = await User.filter(name__startswith="A").order_by("-id")
```

### Getting Single Objects

```python
user = await User.get(id=1)
user = await User.get_or_none(id=1)
```

### Updating

```python
user = await User.get(id=1)
user.name = "Bob"
await user.save()
```

### Deleting

```python
await user.delete()
```

## Lazy Relations

Tortoise uses lazy loading for relationships. Accessing a related field triggers a database query only when needed.

```python
user = await User.get(id=1)
posts = await user.posts  # Triggers query
```

## Transactions

Use `in_transaction()` to run operations in a transaction.

```python
async with in_transaction():
    await User.create(name="Charlie")
    await Post.create(title="Hello", user=user)
```

## Signals

Models support signals for lifecycle events.

```python
from tortoise.signals import pre_save, post_save

@pre_save(User)
async def user_pre_save(sender, instance, using_db, update_fields):
    print(f"Saving user: {instance.name}")

@post_save(User)
async def user_post_save(sender, instance, created, using_db, update_fields):
    if created:
        print(f"User {instance.name} created")
```

## Model Methods

### `save()`

Saves the instance to the database.

```python
await user.save()
```

### `delete()`

Deletes the instance.

```python
await user.delete()
```

### `refresh()`

Refreshes the instance from the database.

```python
await user.refresh()
```

## Advanced Features

### Custom Field Types

You can define custom field types by subclassing `Field`.

### Database Functions

Use `tortoise.functions` for database-level operations.

```python
from tortoise.functions import Count

count = await User.annotate(count=Count("id")).first()
```

### Raw Queries

Use `raw_query()` for complex or non-standard SQL.

```python
result = await User.raw_query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s", "Alice")
```

## Best Practices

- Use `unique_together` and `indexes` to improve performance.
- Use `related_name` to avoid naming conflicts.
- Use `in_transaction()` for atomic operations.
- Avoid loading large datasets without pagination.
- Use `select_for_update()` for row-level locking.

## Example: Complete Model

```python
from tortoise import Model, fields

class Blog(Model):
    id = fields.IntField(pk=True)
    title = fields.CharField(max_length=100)
    content = fields.TextField()
    author = fields.ForeignKeyField("models.User", related_name="blogs")
    tags = fields.ManyToManyField("models.Tag", related_name="blogs")
    created_at = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    updated_at = fields.DatetimeField(auto_now=True)

    class Meta:
        table = "blogs"
        ordering = ["-created_at"]
        unique_together = ("title", "author")
        indexes = ("created_at",)
```

This model defines a blog post with a title, content, author, tags, and timestamps. It uses foreign keys and many-to-many relationships, with proper metadata for database behavior.

Use of __models__

If you define the variable __models__ in the module which you load your
models from, generate_schema will use that list, rather than
automatically finding models for you.

Primary Keys

In Tortoise ORM we require that a model has a primary key.

That primary key will be accessible through a reserved field pk which
will be an alias of whichever field has been nominated as a primary key.
That alias field can be used as a field name when doing filtering e.g.
.filter(pk=...) etc…

Note

We currently support single (non-composite) primary keys of any
indexable field type, but only these field types are recommended:

    IntField
    BigIntField
    CharField
    UUIDField

One must define a primary key by setting a pk parameter to True. If you
don't define a primary key, we will create a primary key of type
IntField with name of id for you.

Note

If this is used on an Integer Field, generated will be set to True
unless you explicitly pass generated=False as well.

Any of these are valid primary key definitions in a Model:

    id = fields.IntField(pk=True)

    checksum = fields.CharField(pk=True)

    guid = fields.UUIDField(pk=True)

Inheritance

When defining models in Tortoise ORM, you can save a lot of repetitive
work by leveraging from inheritance.

You can define fields in more generic classes and they are automatically
available in derived classes. Base classes are not limited to Model
classes. Any class will work. This way you are able to define your
models in a natural and easy to maintain way.

Let's have a look at some examples.

        id = fields.IntField(pk=True)

        class Meta:
            abstract = True

        # from MyAbstractBaseModel
        id = fields.UUIDField(pk=True)

        # Adding additional fields
        first_name = fields.CharField(20, null=True)

            table = "user"

The DB-backing field

Note

A ForeignKeyField is a virtual field, meaning it has no direct DB
backing. Instead it has a field (by default called {FKNAME}_id (that is,
just an _id is appended) that is the actual DB-backing field.

It will just contain the Key value of the related table.

This is an important detail as it would allow one to assign/read the
actual value directly, which could be considered an optimization if the
entire foreign object isn't needed.

Specifying an FK can be done via either passing the object:

    await SomeModel.create(tournament=the_tournament)
    # or
    somemodel.tournament=the_tournament

or by directly accessing the DB-backing field:

    await SomeModel.create(tournament_id=the_tournament.pk)
    # or
    somemodel.tournament_id=the_tournament.pk

underscore, and then the foreign object's field. Then a normal query
attr can be appended. This can be chained if the next key is also a
foreign object:

  {FKNAME}__{FOREIGNFIELD}__gt=3

There is however one major limiatation. We don't want to restrict
foreign column names, or have ambiguity (e.g. a foreign object may have
a field called isnull)

Then this would be entierly ambugious:

To prevent that we require that direct filters be applied to the
DB-backing field of the foreign key:
